newsitem.title: UK: AIRLINERS IN NEAR MISS OVER UK, SAY CONTROLLERS.
newsitem.headline: AIRLINERS IN NEAR MISS OVER UK, SAY CONTROLLERS.

text.p: Two airliners came within 250 yards (metres) of each other over southern England and only quick thinking by an air traffic controller prevented a possible collision, officials said on Thursday.

The near-miss occurred on Tuesday when a Boeing B-737 of the Dutch airline KLM descended too far and came close to a McDonnell Douglas MD-80 of the Scandinavian carrier SAS, the main air traffic controllers' union said.

The incident happened as the two airliners were waiting to land at London's Heathrow airport just hours after 349 people were killed when a Saudi airliner and a Kazakh cargo plane collided over India.
"This was an unusual near-miss. We only reported five incidents of such seriousness last year," said an official from the Institution of Professionals, Managers and Specialists.
The union said the KLM plane, on a flight from Amsterdam, had been cruising at 16,000 feet (4,890 metres) when it was cleared to descend to 15,000 feet (4,575 metres).
But for some reason it continued down to 14,100 feet (4,300 metres), virtually the same altitude as the SAS jet, which had taken off from the Danish town of Aarhus.
"The KLM pilot was given clear instructions which he understood, but for some reason he went through the (15,000 feet) level," the union official said by telephone.
When the jets were just 250 yards apart an air traffic controller realised what was happening and told the KLM pilot to climb immediately to 15,000 feet.
"The combination of technical back-up and air traffic controller response meant that a disaster similar to that in India was averted," the official said.

When the near-miss occurred at 4.39 p.m. (1639 GMT) the skies were particularly crowded because one of the runways at Heathrow was blocked. Poor weather conditions meant it was unlikely the two pilots realised their planes were so close.
The British Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said it had started an investigation after a controller filed a near-miss report. It declined to give any further details.
A KLM spokesman in the Netherlands confirmed the pilot had been asked to change altitude by air traffic control and said the CAA had asked the airline for more information.

In September the pilot of a British Airways airliner with 42 people on board filed a near miss report after he saw a jet fighter flying towards him at the same altitude over northern England just one mile (1.6 km) away.
